title: How the day ended
text: Stocks finished higher. The S&P 500 fund SPY closed at $772.31, up 0.3%, and the Nasdaq 100 fund QQQ closed at $725.61, up 0.6%. The Fed kept interest rates unchanged, and the day's biggest single move on our list was Vertiv, up about 16%. Tomorrow, watch whether chip stocks keep their gains. This is for learning, not advice.

title: The Fed holds rates steady
text: The Federal Reserve left its main interest rate at 3.75% to 4%. Two members voted to raise it a quarter point, which shows some officials still worry about prices rising. Rates are the price of borrowing money, so they touch almost every stock. Stocks ended the day higher, so the news was not a shock.

title: Vertiv leaps on strong sales
text: Vertiv closed at $242.94, up 16.5%. The company said its sales grew 61% and raised its forecast for the year. It makes power and cooling equipment for data centers, so it is one of the 'picks and shovels' of AI. Even after the jump it sits 36% below its 52 week high of $379.94. The 52 week range is the climb from the lowest to the highest price in the past year.

title: AMD is up, but expensive
text: AMD closed at $578.44, up 3.2%. Its P/E ratio is about 147, while Google's is about 17. P/E tells you how many dollars investors pay for each $1 the company earns in a year. A high number means people expect a lot of growth, and big hopes can lead to big drops. AMD also has a beta of 2.45, so it swings much more than the market.

title: Health stocks lead the sectors
text: Among Nasdaq sectors, Healthcare did best today, up 2.1%, and Utilities did worst, down 1.0%. A sector is a group of companies in the same kind of business. Our health picks, Eli Lilly and Intuitive Surgical, moved less than the sector average. Eli Lilly closed at $1,288.78, up 0.5%, and Intuitive Surgical closed at $444.18, down 0.4%.

title: Lesson 27: What is revenue?
text: Revenue is all the money a company brings in from selling things, before it pays any bills. Profit is what is left after paying for workers, parts, and taxes. Imagine a lemonade stand that sells $100 of lemonade but spends $70 on lemons, cups, and sugar. Revenue is $100, and profit is $30. Investors watch revenue growth because a company that sells more each year may keep growing. When Vertiv says its sales rose 61%, that is revenue growth. But growing sales do not always mean growing profit, so it helps to check both.
